reference_title: California Trenching and Shoring Manual (Caltrans, June 2011, Revision 2 - July 2025)

sections.title: Use of Anchor Blocks (Deadmen)
sections.summary: Tie rods can run to anchor blocks (deadmen) behind the excavation face; a block's resistance is the passive pressure developed in front of it. Placement matters (Figure 10-2): a block inside the active wedge offers no resistance; one whose passive wedge overlaps the wall's active wedge has reduced resistance, the reduction becoming load on the wall; blocks further back develop full capacity but increase pressure on the wall. A safety factor of 2 is recommended for all anchor blocks (p. 10-4). In cohesionless soil the Ovesen factor R (3-D / 2-D ultimate load) is used at no more than 2; Tult = R*(Pp - Pa)*L (Eq. 10-2-36 in Example 10-1).
sections.body: Proper placement of anchor blocks (deadmen) is one challenge, and easily overlooked: anchors placed within a soil failure wedge will not provide the resistance value needed when soil movement in the active zone occurs (Section 10-1). An anchor block system's resistance is through the passive pressure developed in front of the block. Figure 10-2: block A, inside the active wedge, offers no resistance; block B's resistance is reduced by the overlap of the wall's active wedge and the block's passive wedge, and the reduced portion becomes load transferred to the wall; blocks C and D develop full capacity but increase pressure on the wall. Anchor blocks should be placed against firm, undisturbed, or recompacted soil, and a safety factor of 2 is recommended for all anchor blocks (p. 10-4). For an isolated/continuous anchor block in cohesionless soil, three-dimensional end effects increase the capacity; Ovesen's theory gives the factor R = (3-D ultimate load)/(2-D ultimate load), and if the calculated R value is more than 2, the R value used should be equal to 2 (Example 10-1, p. 10-15). In Example 10-1 the ultimate anchor-block capacity is Tult = R x (Pp - Pa) x L (Eq. 10-2-36), where L is the block length, and the factor of safety FS = Tult/T is checked against the applied tie load T (the worked example shows FS = 2.03). Cases are given for cohesionless soil at the surface, cohesionless soil with 1.5 <= D/H <= 5.5, and cohesive soil near and below the surface (d <= H/2 and d >= H/2).
key_points: A block inside the active wedge offers no resistance; one overlapping it has reduced resistance; full capacity further back (Figure 10-2)
Resistance comes from the passive pressure in front of the block; Tult = R x (Pp - Pa) x L
Ovesen 3-D factor R = (3-D ultimate)/(2-D ultimate); if it exceeds 2, R = 2 should be used
Check FS = Tult / T on the applied tie load; a safety factor of 2 is recommended for all anchor blocks (p. 10-4)

equations.description: Ultimate anchor-block capacity in Example 10-1: Tult = R x (Pp - Pa) x L, L the block length; R the Ovesen factor, taken as 2 where the calculated value exceeds 2.

sections.title: Heave (Bottom Heave of Braced Cuts in Clay)
sections.summary: Heave can occur in soft plastic clays when the excavation is deep enough to displace the surrounding clay upward; heave and slip circle failure should be checked when the stability number No = gamma*H/c exceeds 6 (Eq. 10-3-1). Terzaghi (1943): driving load Q = W + (0.7B)q - S (Eq. 10-3-2; W = gamma H (0.7B), S = cH) treated as a load on a continuous footing of width 0.7B, resisted by Qu = cNc(0.7B) (Eq. 10-3-3), Nc from Bjerrum & Eide (1956, Figure 10-15). FS = Qu/Q >= 1.5 (Eq. 10-3-5): a minimum safety factor of 1.5 is recommended.
sections.body: Heave occurs in soft plastic clays when the excavation depth displaces surrounding clay vertically with corresponding upward movement of the excavation bottom. The possibility of heave and slip circle failure in soft clays, and in the underlying clay layers, should be checked when the Stability Number No = gamma*H/c exceeds 6 (Eq. 10-3-1). Terzaghi (1943) analyzed the FS of long braced excavations against bottom heave (Figure 10-14). The vertical driving load per unit length along line dc is Q = W + (0.7B)*q - S (Eq. 10-3-2), where W = gamma*H*(0.7B) is the soil column weight, B the open-excavation width, q the surcharge, and S = cH the cohesion resistance over the excavation depth (modeled as a negative driving force). The driving force Q is treated as a load on a continuous footing of width 0.7B; the resisting net ultimate bearing capacity is Qu = c*Nc*(0.7B) (Eq. 10-3-3), with Nc from Bjerrum & Eide (1956, Figure 10-15) varying with H/B and L/B. The factor of safety against heave is FS = FRS/FDR = Qu/Q >= 1.5 (Eq. 10-3-5); to reduce the risk of heave, it is recommended that a minimum safety factor of 1.5 should be used. The FS assumes the clay is homogeneous to at least 0.7B below the bottom of the excavation. If a hard layer is within 0.7B of the bottom, the failure surface depth 0.7B is replaced by the depth D to the hard layer in the W, surcharge, and bearing-capacity terms. Mitigation: extend the sheeting into a more stable layer or for one-half the excavation width (typically valid for H > B), or over-excavate and construct a counterweight; strutting a wall near its bottom will not prevent heave (it only resists the lower shoring sides rotating into the excavation).
key_points: Heave and slip circle failure should be checked when No = gamma*H/c > 6 (Eq. 10-3-1)
Driving force Q = W + 0.7B*q - S; W = gamma*H*0.7B, S = cH (Eq. 10-3-2)
Resisting force Qu = c*Nc*(0.7B) (Terzaghi bearing capacity, Eq. 10-3-3)
Nc from Bjerrum & Eide (1956), function of H/B and L/B (Figure 10-15)
FS = Qu/Q >= 1.5 (Eq. 10-3-5); a minimum safety factor of 1.5 is recommended
Strutting a wall near its bottom will not prevent heave; extend the sheeting or over-excavate and add a counterweight

equations.description: Stability number No = gamma*H/c (heave and slip circle failure should be checked when No exceeds 6).
Heave driving force Q = W + (0.7B)*q - S, with W = gamma*H*(0.7B), S = cH.
Heave resisting force Qu = c*Nc*(0.7B) (Terzaghi bearing capacity).
Factor of safety against bottom heave FS = FRS/FDR = Qu/Q >= 1.5 (a minimum of 1.5 is recommended).

sections.title: Piping (Quick Conditions and Cofferdams)
sections.summary: In pervious sands, piping (quick conditions, sand boils) occurs when an unbalanced hydrostatic head drives upward flow into the excavation bottom; if allowed to continue it transports material, settles adjacent soil and reduces the passive resistance of embedded members. Remedies: equalize the head (let the excavation fill or dewater outside), a seal course (common on Caltrans projects), or embedment long enough that piping should not develop. Drag on a cofferdam (10-4.01): D = (A)(Cd)(gamma_w)V^2/(2g) (Eq. 10-4-1), simplified D = (A)(Cd)(V^2) (Eq. 10-4-2); with the practical Cd = 2.0, D = 2AV^2 (Eq. 10-4-3).
sections.body: For excavations in pervious materials (sands), piping occurs when an unbalanced hydrostatic head exists, driving an upward flow of water into the bottom (also called quick conditions, visible as a sand boil). Continued piping transports material, settles adjacent soil, and reduces the passive resistance of embedded members. One solution is to equalize the unbalanced head by allowing the excavation to fill with water or lowering the water table outside by dewatering (with dewatering the flow rate decreases, the shear strength increases and the soil stops acting as a liquid). On Caltrans projects, one of the common methods to protect or mitigate against piping is a seal course (Foundation Manual, Chapter 12). If the embedded length of the shoring member is long enough, piping should not develop; the USS Steel Sheet Piling Design Manual (p. 65) charts embedment lengths giving an adequate factor of safety against piping. Hydraulic forces on cofferdams (10-4.01): moving water imposes normal forces and eddy forces along the sides of sheet piles (Figure 10-18); the drag force is D = (A)(Cd)(gamma_w)V^2/(2g) (Eq. 10-4-1, Ratay 1984), A the projected area normal to the current (ft^2), Cd the drag coefficient, V the current velocity (ft/s); since gamma_w is about 2g in English units, D = (A)(Cd)(V^2) (Eq. 10-4-2, Cd then in lb-s^2/ft^4); considering the roughness along a sheet pile cofferdam the practical value is Cd = 2.0, D = 2AV^2 (Eq. 10-4-3), applied like a wind load over the projected area (example: 6 ft x 6 ft at 4 ft/s, D = 2(36)(4)^2 = 1,152 lb, 32 psf).
key_points: Piping/quick condition: upward seepage under unbalanced head in pervious sands
Effects: transports material, settles adjacent soil, reduces passive resistance
Mitigate by equalizing the head (flood the cut or dewater outside)
A seal course is a common Caltrans remedy; with long enough embedment piping should not develop
Cofferdam drag: D = (A)(Cd)(gamma_w)V^2/(2g) (Eq. 10-4-1); with Cd = 2.0, D = 2AV^2 (Eq. 10-4-3)

sections.applicability: Controlling piping/quick conditions and hydraulic forces in dewatered or cofferdam excavations

sections.title: Slope Stability
sections.summary: Where the ground surface is not horizontal, gravity may move the soil down the slope. The potential for failure by slippage of the soil around the shoring is present for most shoring types, except two-sided systems in level ground (Section 10-1). A stability analysis by a geotechnical engineer or geologist should be requested from the Contractor when shoring or a cut slope appears to present a possibility of slip failure. Limit-equilibrium methods of slices (Fellenius 1936, Simplified Bishop 1955, Spencer/Janbu) give the lowest FS over trial surfaces; agreement on soil parameters, especially cohesion, is very important, and construction surcharges should be considered.
sections.body: When the ground surface is not horizontal, a gravity component may cause the soil to slide. A stability analysis prepared by a Geotechnical engineer or Geologist should be requested from the Contractor when it appears that shoring or a cut slope presents a possibility of some form of slip failure. Geotechnical Services can perform computer-aided stability analysis to verify a contractor's submitted analysis, and it is recommended the Engineer use this resource for a slope stability review. The potential for slippage of the soil around the shoring is present for most shoring types, the exception being two-sided systems in level ground, i.e. a traditional trench (Section 10-1, p. 10-2). Construction surcharges such as equipment and stockpiled materials may cause excavation instabilities and should be considered in the analysis. The limit-equilibrium method assumes failure when a soil mass slides along a slip surface. The analysis: obtain geometry/stratigraphy/subsurface info, soil properties, soil-structure interaction (sheet/soldier piles, anchors, nails), surcharge loads, then compute the minimum FS against failure for the various stages. Stability is the lowest FS found over multiple trial surfaces; the critical surface is often but not always circular (non-circular surfaces arise from adverse bedding, weak zones, or unfavorable groundwater). Method-of-slices variants: Fellenius Method (Ordinary Method of Slices / Swedish Circle, 1936), Simplified Bishop Method (1955), and Spencer/Janbu. The basic equation for each of these methods is FS = [C_bar*L + tan(phi_bar)*sum(N_bar_i)]/sum(W_i*sin(theta_i)), sums over slices i = 1 to n (Eq. 10-5-1), with C_bar and phi_bar the effective-stress cohesion intercept and friction angle, L the length of the failure arc, N_bar_i the effective normal force, W_i the slice weight and theta_i the base angle. It is very important to be in agreement on the soil parameters with the Contractor, as these have a significant effect on the calculated factor of safety, especially cohesion.
key_points: Slippage around the shoring is possible for most shoring types, except two-sided systems in level ground (Section 10-1)
Method of slices: FS = [C L + tan(phi) sum N_i]/sum(W_i sin theta_i) (Eq. 10-5-1, effective-stress C and phi)
Methods: Fellenius (Swedish Circle, 1936), Simplified Bishop (1955), Spencer/Janbu
Stability = lowest FS over many trial surfaces (circular and non-circular)
Construction surcharges (equipment, stockpiles) should be considered in the analysis
Cohesion strongly affects FS - agree on soil parameters with the Contractor
Request a stability analysis by a geotechnical engineer or geologist from the Contractor when slip failure appears possible

equations.description: Method-of-slices factor of safety FS = [C_bar*L + tan(phi_bar)*sum(N_bar_i)]/sum(W_i*sin(theta_i)), i = 1 to n (effective-stress cohesion intercept and friction angle; L the failure-arc length).
